zh.q: 桌上这些器材各干什么？教材给了哪两个方案？为什么这里根本没有秒表？
zh.concl: 教材 p.10 的方案一（频闪照片或录像，一次拍全所有等时位置）与方案二（斜槽描迹，一次只描一个点）得到的是同一条轨迹；本课走参考案例（p.11 图5.3-2 先做竖直、p.12 图5.3-3 再做水平）。全课没有计时器：时间间隔要靠竖直方向的规律自己定。
points: 器材分四组认：斜槽与钢球 / 竖直比对 / 描迹背板与挡板 / 方格纸与频闪卡。
两个方案的区别只在「记录方式」：一个一次拍全等时位置，一个一次只描一个点。
三个量各有各的来源：v₀ 由落点算、T 由竖直规律算、k 由四点拟合——没有一个时间是被量出来的。

zh.q: 小锤敲下去，A 球平抛、B 球自由下落——谁先落地？换个落台高度、换个击打力度，答案会变吗？
zh.concl: 竖直分运动就是自由落体（初速为零、加速度 g），与水平初速度无关。教材 p.12 只问「从这个实验看，平抛运动在竖直方向的分运动是什么运动？」不给答案——这句话是从 p.11 图5.3-2 的「两球同时落地」推出来的。
points: 竖直分运动与水平初速度无关：换落台高度、换击打力度，两球仍然同时落地。
是「两球同时落地」这一件事把竖直方向的规律钉死成自由落体。
教材用问句收尾（p.12），答案要学生自己从现象里说出来。

zh.q: 教材为什么专门写一句「斜槽 M 末端水平」？不水平的话，第一个坏掉的是什么？
zh.concl: 「末端水平」不是形式要求：只有初速度只有水平分量，竖直方向才是「初速为零的自由落体」，第 5 步的「1 : 4 : 9 : 16」才成立。这是本课那条「错误操作 → 可观察的后果 → 要求解释」。
points: 末端水平就是「v₀ 只有水平分量」；检验办法：把球放在槽口松手，球不动。
上翘 3° 时球自己滚回槽里（a = 0.5129 m/s²），而学生从纸面上看不出来——所以教材要专门写这一句。
它是后面所有「等时」结论的前提，第 8 步还要用它解释偏差。

zh.q: 挡板从 20 mm 升到 320 mm，白纸上会留下四个点。这四个高度为什么正好取这四个数？
zh.concl: 挡板高度取 1 : 4 : 9 : 16 是为了下一步能定出相等的时间间隔（t 比 = 1 : 2 : 3 : 4）；四个点记在白纸上，正是教材「用平滑曲线把这些印迹连接起来」的前一半。
points: 四个挡板高度取 1 : 4 : 9 : 16 不是随便定的，是为了让时间比正好 1 : 2 : 3 : 4。
白纸 + 复写纸记的是球的下缘（这条第 8 步要用）。
同一条刻线内四次落点必须同一个 v₀，换刻线才是换 v₀。

zh.q: 桌上没有计时器。怎么知道钢球落到这四个高度分别用了多长时间？
zh.concl: 「相等的时间间隔」是靠竖直分运动是自由落体这条结论反推出来的（教材 p.12 原句「设法确定『相等的时间间隔』」）——整节课因此不需要计时器。
points: 没有计时器也能有「相等的时间间隔」：全靠 y = ½gt² 反推。
y 比 1:4:9:16 ⟹ t 比 1:2:3:4，第 1 档一下就把 T 定住了。
T = 0.0639 s 与装置尺度自洽：四段飞行一共 0.2556 s。

zh.q: 时间间隔既然相等了，看水平位移——它每次都一样吗？换个画法能看得更清楚吗？
zh.concl: 相等时间内水平位移相等 ⟹ 水平分速度不变（教材 p.12「再看相等的时间内水平分运动的位移」）。竖直方向有什么毛病都改不了水平方向的结论：末端上翘时 Δx 仍是 95.33 / 95.58 / 95.64 mm，坏的只是「这些点等不等时」。
points: Δx 恒定才叫匀速（三个间隔必须一样），不是「看着差不多」。
换画法（横轴档位序号）四点要落在过原点的直线上，这才排除「有初位移」。
水平方向的结论不受竖直方向毛病影响：上翘时 Δx 仍恒定。

zh.q: 把刻线从②换成③，还是这四个挡板档位——四点往哪边跑？连起来的曲线变陡还是变平？
zh.concl: 换 v₀ 只把抛物线整体变陡 / 变平，形状仍是 y = kx²（教材 p.16 式(3)，第 4 节）；k 恒定就是「一条抛物线」的定量说法，而 v₀ = √(g/(2k)) 是第二条测量路，与第 5 条的单点算法必须一致。
points: 换 v₀ 只改抛物线的陡缓，不改「是抛物线」这件事：k 从 2.1778 → 1.2250 → 4.9000。
轨迹方程 y = (g/2v₀²)x² 是第 4 节的内容，本节只要求「看出是同一条曲线」。
由 k 也能反解 v₀，与单点算法必须一致——两条路互相校核。

zh.q: 如果末端翘了一点，或者忘了钢球有半径，四个点还能算出一个 v₀ 吗？偏大还是偏小？
zh.concl: 两种毛病都是系统性偏大，区别在「随档位怎么变」：球半径让越靠上偏得越多（v₀测/v₀ − 1 = √(1 + r/y) − 1），末端上翘让每一档都偏、且 x 比不再是 1:2:3:4。修法：把每个 y 加 r（或把原点下移 r）、把斜槽调回水平。
points: 两种毛病方向相同、随档位的变化不同：球半径「越靠上偏得越多」，末端上翘「每档都偏、且 x 比不再是 1:2:3:4」。
两个偏差都能用一个数说清（+22.61 % / +13.17 %），不是「误差看运气」。
教材把这两件事都写成了问句（p.11「物体的大小对描绘轨迹是否有影响？如何减小这种影响？」），答案要学生给。

zh.q: 给你斜槽、白纸、挡板和方格纸，不许用秒表——能不能把钢球的初速度测出来，让四组数据自己说明它是一致的？
zh.concl: 没有新结论：把前八步连起来用一遍——分解（竖直定时间、水平测速度）+ 抛物线校核。这正是教材 p.11「请设计表格，把所测量的数据填入表格……检验你的猜想」的定量版。
points: 先按 v₀ ≈ x√(g/2y) 估一个数，再看四组是不是同一个数。
四组必须同一条刻线：换刻线会把两个 v₀ 混进一张表。
真实档（球半径未修正）一定测不准——这不是学生算错，是球半径那一项的系统误差。

en.q: What is each piece of equipment on the bench for? Which two methods does the textbook give? Why is there no stopwatch here at all?
en.concl: Textbook p.10's method 1 (strobe photo or video, capturing all equally timed positions at once) and method 2 (tracing with a chute, one point at a time) give the same trajectory; this lesson follows the reference case (vertical first in Fig. 5.3-2 on p.11, then horizontal in Fig. 5.3-3 on p.12). There's no timer anywhere in the lesson: the time interval has to come from the law of vertical motion.
points: Recognize the equipment in four groups: chute and ball / vertical comparison / tracing board and catch board / grid paper and strobe card.
The two methods differ only in "how they record": one captures all equally timed positions at once, the other traces one point at a time.
Each quantity has its own source: v₀ from the landing point, T from the vertical law, k from fitting four points. Not a single time is measured.

en.q: The hammer strikes: ball A is launched horizontally, ball B drops freely. Which lands first? Does the answer change with a different drop height or a harder strike?
en.concl: The vertical component is free fall (zero initial speed, acceleration g), independent of horizontal initial speed. Textbook p.12 only asks "From this experiment, what kind of motion is the vertical component of projectile motion?" without answering; the answer is inferred from "both balls land together" in Fig. 5.3-2 on p.11.
points: The vertical component doesn't depend on horizontal speed: change the drop height or strike strength, and the balls still land together.
It's the single fact "both balls land together" that pins the vertical motion down as free fall.
The textbook ends with a question (p.12); students have to state the answer from what they observe.

en.q: Why does the textbook specifically say "the end of chute M is horizontal"? If it isn't, what breaks first?
en.concl: "End horizontal" isn't a formality: only if the initial velocity is purely horizontal is the vertical motion "free fall from rest", and only then does step 5's "1 : 4 : 9 : 16" hold. This is the lesson's "wrong procedure → visible consequence → explain it".
points: End horizontal means "v₀ is purely horizontal"; to check, place the ball at the exit and let go: it shouldn't move.
Tilted up 3°, the ball rolls back into the chute on its own (a = 0.5129 m/s²), and students can't see that from the paper; that's why the textbook spells it out.
It's the premise of every later "equal time" conclusion, and step 8 uses it to explain deviations.

en.q: Raise the catch board from 20 mm to 320 mm and four marks appear on the paper. Why exactly these four heights?
en.concl: Board heights in the ratio 1 : 4 : 9 : 16 let the next step fix equal time intervals (t ratio = 1 : 2 : 3 : 4); the four points on the paper are the first half of the textbook's "connect the marks with a smooth curve".
points: The four board heights in the ratio 1 : 4 : 9 : 16 aren't arbitrary; they make the time ratio exactly 1 : 2 : 3 : 4.
White paper + carbon paper record the bottom edge of the ball (step 8 needs this).
All four landings for one mark must share the same v₀; changing the mark changes v₀.

en.q: There's no timer on the bench. How do you know how long the ball took to fall to each of these four heights?
en.concl: The "equal time interval" is worked back from the conclusion that the vertical component is free fall (textbook p.12: "find a way to fix 'equal time intervals'"), so the whole lesson needs no timer.
points: You can have "equal time intervals" without a timer: it all comes from working back from y = ½gt².
y ratio 1:4:9:16 ⟹ t ratio 1:2:3:4, and position 1 fixes T at once.
T = 0.0639 s is consistent with the apparatus size: the four flights total 0.2556 s.

en.q: Now that the time intervals are equal, look at the horizontal displacement. Is it the same each time? Would a different plot show it more clearly?
en.concl: Equal horizontal displacements in equal times ⟹ constant horizontal velocity (textbook p.12: "then look at the horizontal displacement in equal times"). No vertical fault can change the horizontal conclusion: with the end tilted up, Δx is still 95.33 / 95.58 / 95.64 mm; what breaks is only "whether these points are equally timed".
points: Uniform means Δx is constant (all three intervals the same), not "looks about equal".
On the alternative plot (x-axis = position number) the four points must lie on a line through the origin; that rules out "an initial offset".
The horizontal conclusion isn't affected by vertical faults: with the end tilted up, Δx is still constant.

en.q: Switch from mark ② to mark ③ with the same four board positions. Which way do the four points move? Does the curve get steeper or flatter?
en.concl: Changing v₀ only makes the whole parabola steeper / flatter; the shape stays y = kx² (textbook p.16, eq. (3), Sec. 4). A constant k is the quantitative way of saying "one parabola", and v₀ = √(g/(2k)) is a second measuring route that must agree with the single-point method in item 5.
points: Changing v₀ only changes how steep the parabola is, not that it is one: k goes 2.1778 → 1.2250 → 4.9000.
The trajectory equation y = (g/2v₀²)x² belongs to Sec. 4; this section only asks you to "see that it's the same curve".
v₀ can also be found from k, and it must agree with the single-point method: the two routes check each other.

en.q: If the end is tilted up slightly, or you forget the ball has a radius, can the four points still give one v₀? Too high or too low?
en.concl: Both faults give systematically high values; they differ in "how it changes across positions": the ball radius biases the upper positions more (v₀_meas/v₀ − 1 = √(1 + r/y) − 1), while an upward tilt biases every position and the x ratio is no longer 1:2:3:4. Fixes: add r to each y (or move the origin down by r), and level the chute.
points: Both faults push the same way but vary differently across positions: the ball radius "biases more higher up", the upward tilt "biases every position, and the x ratio is no longer 1:2:3:4".
Each bias can be stated as a number (+22.61 % / +13.17 %); error is not "luck".
The textbook poses both as questions (p.11: "Does the size of the object affect the traced trajectory? How can the effect be reduced?"), and students supply the answers.

en.q: Given a chute, white paper, a catch board and grid paper, and no stopwatch, can you measure the ball's initial speed and let four data sets show it's consistent?
en.concl: No new conclusion: use the first eight steps together, decomposing (vertical for time, horizontal for speed) + parabola check. This is the quantitative version of textbook p.11: "design a table, fill in the measured data… test your guess".
points: Estimate a value with v₀ ≈ x√(g/2y) first, then see whether the four sets give the same number.
All four sets must use the same release mark: changing marks mixes two v₀ values into one table.
Real mode (ball radius not corrected) will always miss: that isn't a calculation mistake, it's the systematic error from the ball radius.
